newsitem.title: UK: Surge in Chinese zinc exports misleading-Macquarie.
newsitem.headline: Surge in Chinese zinc exports misleading-Macquarie.

text.p: An apparent surge in Chinese zinc output and exports was misleading, so a bull market should resume after prices undergo a temporary correction, broker Macquarie Equities said in a report.

"A short-term correction in zinc prices may be possible if the large tonnages coming out of China end up in the Singapore LME warehouses," said the report, written before Monday's stocks data showed 6,000 tonnes of zinc arrived in the Singapore warehouse.
"This would, in our view, be a temporary correction in a bull market, not a change in direction," it added.
Three month LME prices shed nearly $30 to $1,238 per tonne on Monday's pre-market.

A lot of talk has circulated recently about the imminent arrival of large amounts of Chinese zinc in Singapore. "This was seen by traders as the start of a concerted effort by a group of Chinese smelters, who are rumoured to be short, to talk prices down," Macquarie said.

Chinese customs figures showed exports in January and February of unwrought zinc and zinc alloys shot up 181.6 percent year-on-year to 73,309 tonnes and the State Statistical Bureau said output rose by 37.5 percent to 204,500 tonnes.
"A superficial reading of this information could lead to a significant bear case for zinc," Macquarie said.
But the rise in exports early this year was an anomaly.

"A change in timing of exports in 1996/97 seems to be behind the apparent surge in 1997 exports of zinc. In previous years huge amounts were exported in December to meet export quotes," the report said.
But an export tax was removed at the end of last year, providing an incentive to delay exports into January and February, it added.
If production in January and February 1997 is annualised, the total figure is only six percent higher than total output in 1996, it added.
Some smelters such as Zhuzhou, which has announced plans to increase output and exports, may be able to boost capacity.
"Others will continue to struggle due to capacity limitations and more importantly, a shortage of concentrate feedstock," the broker said.
